paras: The expulsion of Black men from Walnut, Kansas, was a series of incidents in late summer 1903 in which four Black men were chased out of the town of Walnut, which reportedly refused to allow any Black person on its townsite. The episode is known only from a one-sentence item in the Topeka State Journal, which reported it without comment.

According to the State Journal of 12 September 1903, Walnut, which the paper placed in Neosho county, "refuses to allow a negro on the townsite." The same item said that "four colored men have been chased away in the past thirty days," which puts the expulsions between about mid-August and mid-September 1903. The report gave no names for the men, no dates for the individual incidents, and no account of who drove them out or how.
No report of arrests, official action or any protest appears in the coverage, and no later item about Walnut's policy was found.

The item ran in "Jayhawker Jots," the State Journal's column of short Kansas town notes, where it sat among jokes about a six-legged cow, a reporter "seeing white sparrows," and a mattress factory seeking "tufters." The paper presented the exclusion as a flat statement of fact, attributing it to the town as a whole and offering neither criticism nor explanation.
No other white newspaper and no Black newspaper in the searched collections carried the story, so the town's policy and the four expulsions rest on this single sentence.
